skills_learned.writing-commit-messages:
---
name: writing-commit-messages
description: Use when writing a git commit message for a change, especially in repos that enforce conventional-commit (commitlint) rules on the subject, body and ticket footer.
metadata:
  version: 1
  tags: []
  learned_by: myelinate
---

# writing-commit-messages

## Steps
- When writing a commit subject, use conventional-commit format 'type(scope): description' (e.g. 'fix(payments): handle missing webhook signature header'), not plain imperative prose. <!-- b-a8b5e800 -->
- When the change has a ticket, keep a body explaining the fix and end with a footer line 'Refs: <ticket-id>'. <!-- b-967cd403 -->

## Verification
- Before finalizing a commit subject, count its characters and confirm it is 60 characters or fewer, in lower case, with no trailing period; shorten the description if it is longer. <!-- b-b6715b56 -->
skills_learned.writing-database-migrations:
---
name: writing-database-migrations
description: Use when writing a SQL (e.g. PostgreSQL) database migration file for a project whose migration-lint enforces transaction wrapping, idempotent DDL and a rollback section.
metadata:
  version: 2
  tags: []
  learned_by: myelinate
---

# writing-database-migrations

## Steps
- When writing the up part of a migration, wrap all statements in 'BEGIN;' ... 'COMMIT;' rather than emitting bare DDL statements. <!-- b-3fefef50 -->
- When a migration creates a table, an index or a column, use IF NOT EXISTS (CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS, CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS, ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS) so it is idempotent. <!-- b-1d1876e1 -->
- When finishing a migration file, append a '-- down:' section that undoes every up statement with the matching IF EXISTS drop: 'DROP TABLE IF EXISTS <table>;', 'DROP INDEX IF EXISTS <index>;', or 'ALTER TABLE <table> DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS <column>;'. <!-- b-cae557ad -->

## Verification
- Before returning a migration, confirm it has a BEGIN;/COMMIT; wrapper, uses IF NOT EXISTS on every CREATE TABLE/CREATE INDEX/ADD COLUMN, and ends with a '-- down:' rollback section. <!-- b-93eb6da4 -->
skills_learned.writing-customer-support-replies:
---
name: writing-customer-support-replies
description: Use when replying to a customer support ticket or email (e.g. damaged orders, refund requests) where support-qa enforces greeting, ticket reference, refund policy and sign-off conventions.
metadata:
  version: 3
  tags: []
  learned_by: myelinate
---

# writing-customer-support-replies

## Steps
- When starting a support reply, open with exactly 'Hi <FirstName>,' as the first line, with no 'Subject:' line or other text before it. <!-- b-d1f8140c -->
- When referencing the ticket in a support reply, write it as '#<ticket-id>' rather than 'ticket <ticket-id>' or other phrasing. <!-- b-d65abc96 -->
- When closing a support reply, make the exact final line '— Acme Support' (em dash) instead of 'Best regards' or any other conventional sign-off. <!-- b-6cca2946 -->

## Pitfalls
- When a customer asks for a refund or reports a duplicate or erroneous charge (an implicit refund request), never promise, start or confirm a refund or give a timeline; state that the billing team will review it, and ask for the order number and evidence (photos or proof of charges). <!-- b-2acc0224 -->

## Heuristics
- When a customer reports a bug or that a feature (e.g. a discount code) isn't working, acknowledge it and ask for reproduction details (device, OS, browser or app version, screenshot, exact input used), keeping the required greeting, '#<ticket-id>' and sign-off. <!-- b-9763cadc -->

## Verification
- Before sending a support reply, confirm the first line is exactly 'Hi <FirstName>,', the ticket appears as '#<ticket-id>', no refund or timeline is promised, and the last line is exactly '— Acme Support'. <!-- b-5734329c -->
skills_learned.writing-python-functions:
---
name: writing-python-functions
description: Use when writing a Python function or module for a repo checked by python-ci review-bot, which enforces Google-style docstrings with Args:, Returns: and Raises: sections.
metadata:
  version: 2
  tags: []
  learned_by: myelinate
---

# writing-python-functions

## Steps
- When writing a Python function, give it a Google-style docstring: a summary line, then 'Args:' describing each parameter, 'Returns:' with type and meaning, and 'Raises:' listing exceptions, instead of a one-line docstring. <!-- b-aa4704d0 -->
- When input can be empty, malformed or yield a degenerate result (e.g. no usable characters), raise ValueError with a clear message instead of returning a silent default like '' or None; review-bot enforces 'no silent defaults'. <!-- b-ba63c458 -->

## Verification
- Before finishing a Python function, scan its body for every raise (e.g. TypeError for wrong input type, ValueError for malformed input) and confirm each exception appears in the docstring's 'Raises:' section with its condition. <!-- b-131d876d -->
